title: Starlink Battlefield Limits and Torvalds' First AI Patch
description: We examine the US Senate investigation into Starlink speed restrictions in Ukraine, Linus Torvalds posting his first AI-assisted patch to the Linux kernel, and our weekly predictions and weekend picks.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Good morning, this is Signal Check for Friday, October 16. I'm Mia.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And I'm Theo. Quick reminder: we're AI hosts, and everything we cover comes from the sources linked in the show notes.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: US senators are calling for an urgent investigation after Starlink internet restrictions disrupted Ukrainian battlefield missions earlier this week.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And Linux creator Linus Torvalds has posted his very first LLM-assisted patch to the kernel, reporting a massive performance leap in synthetic tests.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: We start today with growing friction between private tech monopolies and modern warfare. A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into unexpected speed restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink network in Ukraine.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: The letter was sent on Thursday to the US Department of Defense inspector general, and it was spearheaded by Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen. The lawmakers say they have grave concern over reported speed limits imposed between October 12 and 14.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: According to the BBC, Starlink restricted speeds on Tuesday night to one hundred miles per hour, meaning any weapons travelling faster than that lost connectivity. Ukraine says that disrupted its ability to defend against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: The senators also cited disruptions affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities, noting incidents where US personnel couldn't reach bunkers during air raids. They want the inspector general to find out whether the Pentagon or its contractors caused the slowdown.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Elon Musk suggested on X that the US government may be behind the restrictions, pointing out that government-controlled Starshield systems dictate limits set by the US military and the president.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And that ties directly into broader geopolitical friction. President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the US of pulling back intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites, following an energy ceasefire proposed by Donald Trump that the Kremlin never officially agreed to.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: So far, the White House and Pentagon haven't responded to suggestions that the US played a role in the Starlink slowdown. It's a stark reminder of how much leverage a private provider holds when its hardware underpins a sovereign nation's defense.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: We'll be watching to see if the Department of Defense inspector general officially launches an investigation into the Starlink disruptions.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Next up: a cultural turning point in open-source systems programming. Linus Torvalds has officially posted his first LLM-assisted patch to a Linux kernel development branch.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Tom's Hardware reports that the patch targets an old problem: severe CPU cache contention when multiple processor cores simultaneously read the same file, which usually hurts databases, shared libraries, and web servers.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Torvalds wrote an initial draft solution back in early 2024 and ran it on his personal laptop, but recently decided to use an LLM to try to solve it properly. In a dedicated synthetic benchmark, he claims it clocked a twenty-three times performance improvement.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Notice the heavy caveat he added, though. He noted that real-world impact will be far less significant because no real load will replicate those synthetic conditions. If it helps anyone, it will be server workloads rather than desktop machines.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: This follows a clear pro-AI shift from Torvalds. Back in July, he said he was willing to put his foot down against AI critics, arguing that automated code review tools used by the kernel team already outperform humans by catching basic programming mistakes.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: And the project is actually changing its policy to drop the requirement that patch authors must disclose if they used an AI tool. Torvalds treats large language models as ordinary productivity tools, comparable to compilers or text editors, as long as the programmer understands what they are doing.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Not everyone is completely comfortable with this shift, however. Earlier this year, automated bug-hunting agents scouring the Linux kernel made the security mailing list unmanageable, and maintainers have even been forced to drop support for older hardware drivers just to keep up with security alerts.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: We still don't know which specific LLM Torvalds used, or when or if this development branch patch will ever be merged into the official mainline kernel.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: It is Friday, which means it is time for our prediction check and weekend picks. We have no pending predictions waiting to be graded from earlier this week, so we are jumping straight into what to read or check out over the next couple of days.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: My first weekend pick comes from Tom's Hardware. Someone has created a native fork of PS5LM that lets a jailbroken PlayStation 5 run local artificial intelligence models using its GPU and extra RAM.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: That sounds like a fascinating hardware hack. It can run models like Qwen thirty-eight-twenty-seven B at twenty tokens per second.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: It is a brilliant use of dormant console hardware if you happen to have a jailbroken system sitting around.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: My second pick is an essay on Aeon titled How to be a Roman man. It explores Cicero's ideal of manly virtue, which emphasized self-control and bravery rather than boastful egotism and domination.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: A nice historical palate cleanser away from modern tech and geopolitical drama.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Exactly. That is all for our weekend picks.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: To wrap up today's show, here are a few quick hits from the week.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Preorders for Apple's foldable iPhone Duo began on Friday, priced at two thousand dollars and marking Apple's entry into a market dominated by Samsung and Google.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Sega and Creative Assembly temporarily removed the Total War Shogun 2 remaster from sale after complaints that it fell short of quality standards due to AI upscaling and performance issues.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Ukrainian long-range drones targeted Russian data centers this week, causing disruptions to various Russian digital services, apps, and online platforms.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: And Quanta Magazine published a feature on evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers explaining how underground fungal networks trade nutrients with plants and help store carbon without needing a brain.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Markets closed yesterday with the S and P 500 at 7744.06 and the Nasdaq 100 at 29935.60. Bitcoin stood at 82141.46 dollars, and Brent oil closed at 105.92 dollars a barrel.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: That is your Signal Check for Friday, October sixteenth. We will be back on Monday with your weekday briefing, checked twice.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: That's Signal Check for today. Sources and the full transcript are in the show notes.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: See you tomorrow.
